{{Short description|Chinese government policy encouraging hostility to perceived biological pests}}

[[File:Kill bird and insect.jpg|thumb|Chinese poster reading "Exterminate The Four Pests" (Chinese: 除四害; pinyin: Chú Sì Hài), 1958.]]

The '''Four Pests campaign''' ({{lang-zh|c={{linktext|除|四|害}}|p=Chú Sì Hài}}) was one of the first campaigns of the [[Great Leap Forward]] in [[History of the People's Republic of China (1949–1976)|Maoist China]] from 1958 to 1962. Authorities targeted four "[[Pest (organism)|pests]]" for elimination: [[rat]]s, [[flies]], [[mosquito]]es, and [[Old World sparrow|sparrow]]s.

The extermination of sparrows – also known as the [[Eliminate Sparrows campaign]] – resulted in severe [[ecological]] imbalance, and was one of the causes of the [[Great Chinese Famine]] which lasted from 1959 to 1961, with an estimated death toll due to starvation ranging in the tens of millions (15 to 55 million).{{refn|group="note"|According to various sources.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Smil|first=Vaclav|date=18 December 1999|title=China's great famine: 40 years later|journal=BMJ: British Medical 2020|url-status=live}}</ref>}} In 1960, the campaign against sparrows ended, and [[Cimex|bed bug]]s replaced them as an official target.

== Background ==
The eradication of the four pests together was first mentioned in [[Mao Zedong]]'s ''17-Point Agriculture Policy'', in 1955,{{Refn|also known as the ''Seventeen-Article Document Concerning Agriculture''|group=note}}<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Sheng |first1=Zhao |url=https://brill.com/display/title/33089 |title=Medicine, Health and Social Welfare in Post-1949 China |last2=Zhiliang |first2=Su |publisher=[[Brill (publisher)|Brill]] |year=2025 |isbn=978-90-04-73799-0 |editor-last=Bu |editor-first=Liping |series=Historical Studies of Contemporary China, Volume 5 |location=Leiden |pages=135–149 |translator-last=Xiaoqin |translator-first=Zhang |chapter=Chapter 10: The "Eradicating Four Pests" Campaign of the People's Republic of China |doi=10.1163/9789004737990_011 |editor-last2=Fang |editor-first2=Xiaoping |translator-last2=Yiyang |translator-first2=Li |chapter-url=https://brill.com/display/book/9789004737990/BP000018.xml}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=136}} as a way to reduce infectious diseases and grain loss caused by pests''.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=137}}'' In January 1956, the 17-point policy was expanded into the draft of ''National Programme for Agricultural Development (1956–1967)'', which mentioned that "starting from 1956, we should work to eradicate rats, sparrows, flies, and mosquitoes in all areas possible across the country within five, seven or twelve years".<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=137}} The draft was adopted by the [[Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party]] in 1957, with the timeline revised to twelve years.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=140}}

Among other factors, the failure of food production during the Great Leap Forward was caused by newly mandated agricultural practices imposed by the state. In December 1958, [[Mao Zedong]] created the {{Ill|Eight Elements Constitution|zh|八字宪法}}, eight pieces of agricultural advice purportedly based on science, which were then adopted throughout China. Contrary to expectations, most of the elements decreased agricultural production.<ref name="CW">{{Cite journal |last=Chen |first=Yixin |date=2009 |title=Cold War Competition and Food Production in China, 1957-1962 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/20454912 |journal=Agricultural History |volume=83 |issue=1 |pages=51–78 |doi=10.3098/ah.2008.83.1.51 |issn=0002-1482 |jstor=20454912 |pmid=19618528 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Campaign==
[[File:Eradicate pests and diseases and build happiness for ten thousand generations.jpg|thumb|"Eradicate pests and diseases and build happiness for ten thousand generations" (1960). A poster used during the Four Pests Campaign, in which sparrows had been replaced by bed bugs.]]

The "Four Pests" campaign was introduced as a hygiene campaign aimed to eradicate the pests responsible for the transmission of [[Infection|pestilence]] and [[disease]]:
* the mosquitos responsible for [[malaria]]
* the rodents that spread the [[Plague (disease)|plague]]
* the pervasive airborne flies
* the sparrows—specifically the [[Eurasian tree sparrow]]—which ate [[grain]], seed, and fruit<ref>{{cite news |date=26 February 2014 |title=Paved With Good Intentions: Mao Tse-Tung's "Four Pests" Disaster – Body Horrors |url=https://www.discovermagazine.com/health/paved-with-good-intentions-mao-tse-tungs-four-pests-disaster |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191120144010/http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/bodyhorrors/2014/02/26/mao-four-pests-china-disease/#.WP7DeJMrJE4 |archive-date=20 November 2019 |access-date=25 April 2017 |work=Discover Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref>

Though efforts to eradicate the pests were already well underway in 1957, the campaign would not be officially launched until February 12, 1958.<ref>{{Cite book |last=MacFarquhar |first=Roderick |author-link=Roderick MacFarquhar |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=d9K8X9kKF1cC |title=The origins of the cultural revolution |publisher=[[Columbia University Press]] |year=1983 |isbn=0-231-05716-4 |volume=2 The Great Leap Forward 1958-1960}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=24}} The campaign peaked in the 1957/1958 winter, and a February 1958 article in ''[[The People's Daily]]'' mentioned:<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=143}}

{{Blockquote|text=more than 300 million rats and sparrows, and more than 246,000 [[catties]] (4.54 million boxes) of mosquitoes and flies had been eliminated. More than 3,392,000 catties of fly larvae had been killed. Tens of millions of tons of garbage had been removed. The sanitary condition in urban and rural areas had been greatly improved}}

Activity began decreasing in the second half of 1958, due to the effects of the [[Great Leap Forward]]. In 1960, sparrows were replaced with bed bugs, and a number of city initiatives were aimed towards the campaign.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=|pages=143–144}} However, the collapsing economy meant the campaign was rarely carried out after 1961.<ref name=":0" />{{Reference page|page=145}}

In 1958, the government reported nearly 1.9 billion rats, and nearly 2 billion sparrows were killed.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Wilson |first=Dick |url=https://archive.org/details/anatomyofchinain0000unse/page/134/mode/2up |title=Anatomy of China: An Introduction to One Quarter of Mankind |publisher=[[New American Library|Mentor Books]] |year=1969 |edition=2nd revised |pages=135 |lccn=68-14095}}</ref> In 1959, the campaign reportedly killed over 1 billion sparrows, 1.5 billion rats, 100 million kilograms (200 million pounds) of flies, and 11 million kilograms (25 million pounds) of mosquitoes, though the reliability of these figures are questionable.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lampton |first=David M. |date=1972 |title=Public Health and Politics in China's past Two Decades |journal=Health Services Reports |volume=87 |issue=10 |pages=895–904 |doi=10.2307/4594695 |jstor=4594695 |pmid=4568170 |pmc=1615984 |issn=0090-2918}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Russell |first=Maud |author-link=Maud Russell (social worker) |date=c. 1961 |title=Medicine and Public Health in the People's Republic of China |url=https://www.bannedthought.net/Magazines/FER/1961/FER-1961-MedicineAndPublicHealthInThePRC-MaudRussell-OCR-sm.pdf |journal=[[Far East Reporter]] |pages=9}}</ref>

== Consequences ==

The sparrow campaign ended in disaster, although the other three anti-pest campaigns may have contributed to the improvement in health statistics in the 1950s.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Benson |first1=Linda |title=China Since 1949 |date=2013 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |page=32 |doi=10.4324/9781315833408}}</ref> By April 1960, [[Chinese Communist Party]] leaders changed their opinion on the [[Eliminate Sparrows campaign]] in part due to the influence of [[ornithologist]] [[Tso-hsin Cheng]]<ref>{{cite journal |year=2002 |title=Erinnerungen an Ornithologen, die ich kannte (4. Teil) |trans-title=Reflections on Ornithologists whom I used to know (Part 4) |url=https://www.ala-schweiz.ch/images/stories/pdf/ob/2002_99/OrnitholBeob_2002_99_49_Nowak.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Der Ornithologische Beobachter |language=de |volume=99 |pages=49–70 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210607191716/https://www.ala-schweiz.ch/images/stories/pdf/ob/2002_99/OrnitholBeob_2002_99_49_Nowak.pdf |archive-date=7 June 2021 |access-date=6 June 2021 |author-last=Nowak |author-first=Eugeniusz}}</ref> who pointed out that sparrows ate a large number of insects, as well as grains.<ref>{{cite book |author-last=Shapiro |author-first=Judith Rae |title=Mao's War Against Nature: Politics and the Environment in Revolutionary China |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2001 |isbn=0-521-78680-0}}</ref><ref name="McCarthy">{{cite news |date=2 August 2006 |title=The secret life of sparrows |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/environment/the-secret-life-of-sparrows-410252.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101220145154/http://www.independent.co.uk/environment/the-secret-life-of-sparrows-410252.html |archive-date=20 December 2010 |access-date=30 January 2009 |newspaper=The Independent |author-last=McCarthy |author-first=Michael}}</ref> [[Mao Zedong]] ordered the campaign against sparrows to end, replacing them with [[bedbug]]s.<ref>{{Cite book |author-last=Schmalzer |author-first=Sigrid |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZQuZCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA248 |title=Red Revolution, Green Revolution: Scientific Farming in Socialist China |date=2016 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=978-0-226-33029-7 |page=248 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |author-last=Huang |author-first=Yanzhong |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PHbpTRCRxyMC&pg=PA147 |title=Governing Health in Contemporary China |date=2015 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-136-15548-2 |pages=147 |language=en}}</ref><ref
